board_description: This is a board dedicated to aLOG GRAVITYbot summaries of LIGO activity at two different laboratories: (1) Hanford, Washington (LHO) and (2) Livingston (LLO) near Baton Rouge, Louisiana. The observatories' electronic logbooks provide highly granular accounts of activities and environmental issues surrounding LIGO's interferometers. The summaries below are open for discussion around how these activities and environmental issues influence their operation and sensitivity and may contribute to glitches - or mitigate them.
comment_body:
This summary, along with [the one that preceded it](+tab+/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/6945/3796287) and [the one before that from a week earlier](+tab+/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/6945/3792714), once again paint a quite distorted picture of recent events at LHO - missing the elephant in the room while describing its toenails and the tip of its tail as "crucial", so to speak.

The full story spans *almost a hundred* logbook entries, *not* counting comments. I'll refrain from providing a complete list here (unless someone is keenly interested - but then you can always go to [the source](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/) yourself! ;)), but I'm going to pick out a few of the more important aspects, and one in particular that bears on the fallout in terms of Gravity Spy glitch subjects.

On Wednesday 2025-09-10 a few minutes after noon PDT (= 19:00 UTC), an issue with a 115 kV grid line caused a breaker at the Benton substation (SE of Hanford) to trip open and then close again, resulting in a brief but thorough power outage at the observatory ([LHO:86827](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86827)).

This took out most of the subsystems, and at first the recovery (following a well-established playbook routine) proceeded smoothly ([LHO:86826](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86826) has a timeline attached as a [text file](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/uploads/86826_20250910154011_outage_notes.txt)). Those parts of the Control and Data acquisition System (CDS) - computers and interface devices and the networks connecting them - which weren't protected by Uninterruptible Power Supplies came first, since most everything else depends on them. The main PreStabilized Laser (PSL) was restarted ([LHO:86835](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86835)), as were the CO~2~ lasers and associated chillers of the Thermal Compensation System (TCS) ([LHO:86830](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86830)). The set points of all the many feedback control loops governing the alignment of the optics were restored to sane values ([LHO:86834](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86834)). After dealing with some issues surrounding the Input Mode Cleaner (originating in the IMC's control electronics), LHO managed to reacquire the lock and resume observing - with reduced sensitivity - at around 8pm local time (around 03:00 UTC on 2025-09-11, [LHO:86844](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86844)).

One detail that's implicit in the logbook entries so far, but alluded to in LHO:86844, is that restoring the set points of the control loops does *not* exactly restore the previous beam alignment, due to hysteresis in a number of piezo-actuated mirrors on the PSL table and along the path from the PSL to the IMC. (This difficulty has been known for a long time. See [LHO:7736](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=7736) from 2013, among others.)

With hindsight, the decision to leave the interferometer unattended under Guardian automation control overnight was a little daring - the next several owl shifts were cancelled (and the evening shifts cut short) for fear that a lockloss and subsequent automated reacquisition attempt in this imperfectly aligned state might cause additional damage ([LHO:86870](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86870)). LHO did keep observing the first night until about 17:40 UTC (as is evident from later plots), but afterwards did not reach the Nominal Low Noise state again until Monday 2025-09-15 for just one hour ([LHO:86954](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86954)) and then Tuesday afternoon 2025-09-16 ([LHO:86980](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86980), with one badly rung-up violin mode, but that's [another story](+tab+/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/762/3428271?comment=6215226)).

From Thursday 2025-09-11 until Tuesday 2025-09-16, a number of subsystems where *thoroughly* investigated and adjusted (uncovering and dealing with a few minor pre-existing issues alongside). I'm going to skip over most of these. Yet another [M 7.4 Kamchatka earthquake](+tab+https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us7000qvw5/executive) on Friday added some excitement of its own.

After some remote checks of the PSL and remotely controlled alignment tweaks ([LHO:86882](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86882)), there were two incursions into the PSL enclosure: One on Monday 2025-09-15 to visually inspect the alignment on the optical table and to look for anything else that might be amiss ([LHO:86949](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86949), illustrated with photos), and another on Tuesday to tune the light path to the Reference Cavity that's part of laser-frequency/wavelength stabilization ([LHO:86972](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86972)).

Before and after these activities, numerous measurements were taken of the light sent towards the IMC, the cleaned light transmitted by the IMC, and the junk light rejected (reflected) by it, of which there was rather too much at first - three times as much as before the power outage. On Friday 2025-09-12, an intervention on the optical table ([IOT2L](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/uploads/84149_20250428114303_IMG_2068.jpg)) which hosts in-air photodiodes and wavefront sensors complementing the in-vacuum ones in the adjacent HAM2 and HAM1 chambers changed how much of the IMC REFL beam power was directed towards the relevant PD (planned in [LHO:86880](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86880), executed in [LHO:86884](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86884)) so as to have 1.2 mW instead of 2.4 mW reaching this PD with 2 W incident on the IMC during lock acquisition (implying about 30 mW on the PD at 60 W into the IMC during normal operation), since the PD had been close to saturating before this change. This is one logbook entry that the summarizer *has* picked up, but it missed the context and rationale.

Now let's come to the glitches. First thing Thursday morning local time (2025-09-11), the Detector Characterization experts noticed that the night had come with an "extreme rate of glitching" ([LHO:86848](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86848)) witnessed by `H1:IMC-WFS_A_DC_YAW_OUT_DQ` and a number of other channels, "close to 1 glitch with SNR > 8 every 10 seconds, an increase in rate of 2 orders of magnitude compared to the day before." (Watch out for subjects with numbers in the 113166xxx range: these come from that night.)

On Tuesday 2025-09-16 after reaching Nominal Low Noise again, it was confirmed that the glitches had disappeared again - and this was attributed to the halved power on the IMC REFL photodiode ([LHO:86968](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=86968)). The implication is that the glitches may have originated somewhere in the path from this PD, through its preamplifier and analog electronics and analog-to-digital converter, into the (digital) feedback controls. (*Nota bene*, *not* in the IMC wavefront sensors - these had merely witnessed the glitches.)

Other factors that could have affected the glitch rate had also been investigated in the meantime, and had been found to play only minor roles. But this upgraded summary is getting long enough, so I'm going to leave it at that for now.

comment_body:
Re [LLO:78561](+tab+(+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78561): The offending power supply had already been replaced in the meantime.

Re [LLO:78558](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78558): See [Wikipedia](+tab+https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crowbar_%28circuit%29) for how a "crowbar" protection circuit works and for where the name comes from.

Re [LLO:78676](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78676):
- GDS = Global Diagnostics System (not "Station").
- ETMY = End Test Mass of the Y arm. (Our bot is growing old and already forgetting the most basic acronyms...?)

The (missing) context here is that the finest level of the actuation that keeps the differential arm length (DARM) constant to better than 1 pm had been switched over from ETMX to ETMY in August ([LLO:78071](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78071), [78216](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78216)). The strength of the electrostatic actuation - how much force is applied to the test mass for a given digitally commanded voltage sent to the ESD - is somewhat variable on time scales of hours to weeks (owing to charge build-up on the test mass) and needs to be measured so it can be taken into account.

Moreover, pushing or pulling on ETMY from behind the test mass has the same effect on DARM, respectively, as pulling or pushing on ETMX from behind. Thus the switch from ETMX to ETMY actuation also changed the sign of the calibration factor. This had been compensated in a preliminary way at first; the required modification was finalized during the work reported in [LLO:78676](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78676).

comment_body:
The bot still has deeply entrenched difficulties with the fundamentals of control theory. On the one hand, it overemphasizes "sensor" issues and "alterations" - but sensors are just *one* part of feedback control loops, along with amplifiers, filters, ADCs and DACs, actuators, and digital models of what's being actuated. Radio Frequency signals *aren't* "sensors". The Power Recycling Gain isn't a "sensor". (It's a figure of merit, inferred from sensing other things.) On the other hand, while the DHARD pitch and yaw degrees of freedom of the laser beams in the long arms aren't sensors either, the handoff which occurs during lock acquisition does not "involve[] transitioning *control* of mirrors" - it does involve handing off the *input* of the relevant control loops from one set of sensors to another.

---
What was reported in [LLO:78853](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78853) is totally misrepresented in this summary.

The gain of the laser Intensity Stabilization (not "Integrated Services") Servo's second-level feedback control loop is itself under automation control, and the automation sometimes sees fit to tweak it during the lock acquisition sequence. This has nothing to do with "changes, which weren't monitored or planned" (insinuating human errors) and moreover, being part of the lock acquisition, they would "influence the stability of the system and the quality of the data collected" only in the sense of facilitating the lock acquisition and improving the stability during the subsequent lock stretch.

What the logbook entry is about is something else entirely - the `L1:PSL-ISS_SECONDLOOP_GAIN` channel setting used to be a *monitored* value in the Settings Definition Files (SDF), thus any change of this value from one lock stretch to the next would result in preventing the automation from resuming Observing automatically once lock acquisition had been successfully completed, reaching the nominal low noise state, until a human had reviewed and OK'd the change and any other pending SDF updates. During unattended night shifts, this used to involve an automated phone message to wake up the on-call operator, who then had to log in remotely and click the right buttons - wasting valuable time that could already have been spent Observing. Removing the channel from SDF monitoring means that when there are no other (monitored) SDF differences after a lock reacquisition, Observing can resume at once and automatically.

What prompted this action had been a whole series of locklosses during the preceding day shift ([LLO:78851](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=78851)).

Re [LHO:87431](+tab+https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=87431): Calibration measurements happen regularly at each observatory; executing them simultaneously at LHO and LLO is advantageous (when convenient) but isn't "crucial". It's more important to conduct them on well-thermalized interferometers, rather than shortly after a lock reacquisition.

A calibration sweep involves an interruption to Observing. There's a tradeoff here between maximizing the time when at least one GW observatory is Observing (which may catch a candidate that might otherwise have been missed, but with poor sky localization), versus maximizing the time when two or more are Observing simultaneously (which produces much better sky localizations). During O4, the latter has usually been given precedence.

Re [LLO:79140](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=79140): Oh dear - particle counts reading **zero** in all three size ranges are most assuredly not an "issue". They are the very opposite - a cleanroom that's as clean as it gets! The only conceivable concern here would be whether the dust particle counter is actually working. You'll have to look at the whole *series* of logbook entries about the cleanroom work that has been ongoing for weeks (assembling new components that are going to be installed for O5; it has *nothing* to do with ongoing O4 operations) to see that, firstly, *every* such entry diligently reports the particle counts at the beginning and end of each session, and secondly, they do not always all read zero (but they've never risen enough to be a concern).

Re [LLO:79085](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=79085): Some temperature, humidity, and dew point sensors in the Y arm beam tube enclosure have been faulty for months. Big deal (not). This does not affect observations in any way. (The only concern here is adequate monitoring to prevent an onset of corrosion of the beam tube itself.) It would help if GRAVITYbot wasn't so fixated on everything with "sensor" in its name...

Re [LLO:79153](+tab+https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=79153): Again, this is part of ongoing component assembly work for O5. The blade springs being adjusted here are part of a suspension that is *yet to be completed*, let alone installed in the interferometer.

(The other items here are a bit out of context, they still lack accurate date/time stamps and they still lack logbook entry numbers that would be searchable in Zooniverse Talkl, and they are once again marred by the inappropriate "Dataset 2" verbiage, but at least not blatantly wrong...)
